newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq, U.N. in lengthy tug-of-war over weapons.
newsitem.headline: Iraq, U.N. in lengthy tug-of-war over weapons.

text.p: United Nations arms envoy Rolf Ekeus and senior Iraqi officials are haggling again over small but significant issues which if resolved might eventually lead to a resumption of Iraq's oil exports.

Ekeus, the Swedish head of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) dealing with Iraq, arrived in Baghdad on Saturday and the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) said he met Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz later in the day.

Others including Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf, Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed, who formerly headed Iraq's Military Industrialisation Commission, and presidential adviser General Saadi Tu'ma Abbas were present, INA said.

Sources close to the meetings said the Iraqis pressed for an all-clear from the envoy in the hope of having the curbs on oil exports removed, while Ekeus sought evidence of Baghdad's claims to have done everything asked of it by the outside world.

Lifting the oil export ban, part of sanctions imposed for Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait, is tied to Iraq's coming clean about former biological, chemical and nuclear weapons programmes as well as missiles with ranges beyond 150 km (90 miles).
Ekeus has vowed to deny Iraq his seal of approval unless he knows precisely what happened to missing chemical and biological arms and about a dozen long-range missiles.
Iraq says it has destroyed the prohibited weapons, saying the price it pays for sanctions is more than concealing insignificant amounts of proscribed materials would be worth.
UNSCOM told the U.N. Security Council this month that the missing amounts, while small, raised questions over Iraq's aims.
"It is a real matter of life and death for the states in the region, and therefore we cannot rest until we have accounted for them," Ekeus told reporters in Manama on Friday.
Last June Aziz and Ekeus agreed to work together to close gaps in the weapons files so that UNSCOM could give Baghdad a clean bill of health, a key condition for resuming oil exports.

Ekeus's deputy, Charles Duelfer, who was in Baghdad this month, described Iraqi disclosures of past weapons programmes made after the June pact as flawed and incomplete. Baghdad submitted nine more letters to try to clarify the issues.
Since starting his search in April 1991, Ekeus has sent 373 inspection teams to Iraq with 3,574 inspectors.
Helicopters with monitoring gear helped hunt for weapons and documents. U.S. intelligence reports, satellite pictures and surveillance by U.S. spy planes also aided the effort.
On the ground, Ekeus has set up the most advanced monitoring mechanism to date to check that Iraq's arms industry churns out no banned materials.
Diplomats and analysts in Baghdad believe Iraq will in the end get a clean bill of health from Ekeus but doubt whether this would automatically give it the freedom to export oil freely.

The United States, they say, will view weapons destruction as only one of several conditions Iraq must fulfil, although the relevant Security Council resolution shows that other demands do not apply to oil sales.
Under U.S. pressure, the U.N. put on hold a deal it signed with Baghdad in May that would have permitted Iraq to sell limited amounts of oil for humanitarian purposes.
"If Ekeus declares Iraq clean of weapons, then a clash between the U.S. on the one hand and France and Russia on the other will become inevitable," said one European diplomat.
Both Paris and Moscow are owed billions of dollars by Iraq and have commercial reasons for wanting to see it solvent again.
